entries.188753a495b2f6a1b0766448f26c449fbc872fae: <div sID="gen19773" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Hos.6" sID="Hos.6"/> <div eID="gen19773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19774" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19775" type="x-p"/> The closing words of the foregoing chapter gave us some hopes that God and his Israel, notwithstanding their sins and his wrath, might yet be happily brought together again, that they would seek him and he would be found of them; now this chapter carries that matter further, and some join the beginning of this chapter with the end of that, "They will seek me early," saying, "Come and let us return." But God doth again complain of the wickedness of this people; for, though some did repent and reform, the greater part continued obstinate. Observe, I. Their resolution to return to God, and the comforts wherewith they encourage themselves in their return, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1-Hos.6.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The instability of many of them in their professions and promises of repentance, and the severe course which God therefore took with them, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4-Hos.6.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. The covenant God made with them, and his expectations from them (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">ver. 6</reference>); their violation of that covenant and frustrating those expectations, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.7-Hos.6.11">ver. 7-11</reference>.
entries.41e9f57c518629a9864c3f217febc73afae20041: <div eID="gen19775" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19774" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Penitential Resolutions; Promises. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen19776" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Come, and let us return unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up. <hi type="super">2</hi> After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then shall we know, <hi type="italic">if</hi> we follow on to know the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : his going forth is prepared as the morning; and he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter <hi type="italic">and</hi> former rain unto the earth. <div eID="gen19776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19777" type="x-p"/> These may be taken either as the words of the prophet to the people, calling them to repentance, or as the words of the people to one another, exciting and encouraging one another to <hi type="italic">seek the Lord,</hi> and to humble themselves before him, in hopes of finding mercy with him. God had said, <hi type="italic">In their affliction they will seek me;</hi> now the prophet, and the good people his friends, would strike while the iron was hot, and set in with the convictions their neighbours seemed to be under. Note, Those who are disposed to turn to God themselves should do all they can to excite, and engage, and encourage others to return to him. Observe, <div eID="gen19777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19778" type="x-p"/> I. What it is they engage to do: "<hi type="italic">Come, and let us return to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">v. 1</reference>. Let us go no more to the Assyrian, nor send to king Jareb; we have had enough of that. But let us <hi type="italic">return to the Lord,</hi> return to the worship of him from our idolatries, and to our hope in him from all our confidences in the creature." Note, It is the great concern of those who have revolted from God to return to him. And those who have gone from him by consent, and in a body, drawing one another to sin, should by consent, and in a body, return to him, which will be for his glory and their mutual edification. <div eID="gen19778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19779" type="x-p"/> II. What inducements and encouragements to do this they fasten upon, to stir up one another with. <div eID="gen19779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19780" type="x-p"/> 1. The experience they had had of his displeasure: "Let us return to him, for <hi type="italic">he has torn, he has smitten.</hi> We have been torn, and it was he that tore us; we have been smitten, and it was he that smote us. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> let us return to him, because it is for our revolts from him that he has torn and smitten us in anger, and we cannot expect that he should be reconciled to us till we return to him; and for this end he has afflicted us thus, that we might be wrought upon to return to him. His hand will be stretched out still against us if the people <hi type="italic">turn not to him that smites them,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12-Isa.9.13">Isa. ix. 12, 13</reference>. Note, The consideration of the judgments of God upon us and our land, especially when they are tearing judgments, should awaken us to return to God by repentance, and prayer, and reformation. <div eID="gen19780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19781" type="x-p"/> 2. The expectation they had of his favour: "He that has torn will <hi type="italic">heal us,</hi> he that has smitten will <hi type="italic">bind us up,</hi>" as the skilful surgeon with a tender hand binds up the broken bone or bleeding wound. Note, The same providence of God that afflicts his people relieves them, and the same Spirit of God that convinces the saints comforts them; that which is first <hi type="italic">a Spirit of bondage</hi> is afterwards <hi type="italic">a Spirit of adoption.</hi> This is an acknowledgement of the power of God (he can heal though we be ever so ill torn), and of his mercy (he will do it); nay, <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he has torn that he may heal. Some think this points particularly to the return of the Jews out of Babylon, when they sought the Lord, and joined themselves to him, in the prospect of his gracious return to them in a way of mercy. Note, It will be of great use to us, both for our support under our afflictions and for our encouragement in our repentance, to keep up good thoughts of God and of his purposes and designs concerning us. Now this favour of God which they are here in expectation of is described in several instances:— <div eID="gen19781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19782" type="x-p"/> (1.) They promise themselves that their deliverance out of their troubles should be to them as <hi type="italic">life from the dead</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">After two days he will revive us</hi> (that is, in a short time, in a day or two), <hi type="italic">and the third day,</hi> when it is expected that the dead body should putrefy and corrupt, and be buried <hi type="italic">out of our sight,</hi> then will he <hi type="italic">raise us up,</hi> and <hi type="italic">we shall live in his sight,</hi> we shall see his face with comfort and it shall be reviving to us. Though he <hi type="italic">forsake</hi> for <hi type="italic">a small moment,</hi> he will <hi type="italic">gather</hi> with <hi type="italic">everlasting kindness.</hi>" Note, The people of God may not only be torn and smitten, but left for dead, and may lie so a great while; but they shall not always lie so, nor shall they long lie so; God will in a little time revive them; and the assurance given them of this should engage them to return and adhere to him. But this seems to have a further reference to the resurrection of Jesus Christ; and the time limited is expressed by <hi type="italic">two days</hi> and the <hi type="italic">third day,</hi> that it may be a type and figure of Christ's rising the <hi type="italic">third day,</hi> which he is said to do <hi type="italic">according to the scriptures,</hi> according to this scripture; for all the prophets testified of <hi type="italic">the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow.</hi> Let us see and admire the wisdom and goodness of God, in ordering the prophet's words so that when he foretold the deliverance of the church out of her troubles he should at the same time point out our salvation by Christ, which other salvations were both figures and fruits of; and, though they might not be aware of this mystery in the words, yet now that they are fulfilled in the letter of them in the resurrection of Christ it is a confirmation to our faith that <hi type="italic">this is he that should come,</hi> and we are to <hi type="italic">look for no other.</hi> And it is every way suitable that a prophecy of Christ's rising should be thus expressed, "He will raise <hi type="italic">us</hi> up, and <hi type="italic">we</hi> shall live," for Christ rose as the first-fruits, and we revive with him, we live through him; he rose for our justification, and all believers are said to be <hi type="italic">risen with Christ.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa. xxvi. 19</reference>. And it would serve for a comfort to the church then, and an assurance that God would raise them out of their low estate, for in his fulness of time he would raise his Son from the grave, who would be the life and glory of his people Israel. Note, A regard by faith to a rising Christ is a great support to a suffering Christian, and gives abundant encouragement to a repenting returning sinner; for he has said, <hi type="italic">Because I live, you shall live also.</hi> <div eID="gen19782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19783" type="x-p"/> (2.) That then they shall improve in the knowledge of God (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then shall we know, if we follow on to know, the Lord. Then,</hi> when God returns in mercy to his people and designs favour for them, he will, as a pledge and fruit of his favour, give them more of the knowledge of himself; the earth shall be <hi type="italic">full of that knowledge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Isa. xi. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Knowledge shall be increased,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">Dan. xii. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">All shall know God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">Jer. xxxi. 34</reference>. <hi type="italic">We shall know, we shall follow to know, the Lord,</hi> (so the words are); and it may be taken as the fruit of Christ's resurrection, and the life we live in God's sight by him, that we shall have not only greater means of knowledge, but grace to improve in knowledge by those means. Note, When God designs mercy for a people he gives them <hi type="italic">a heart to know him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.24.7">Jer. xxiv. 7</reference>. Those that have <hi type="italic">risen with Christ</hi> have the spirit of wisdom and revelation given them. And if we understand our living in his sight, as the Chaldee paraphrast does, of the day of the resurrection of the dead, it fitly follows, <hi type="italic">We shall know, we shall follow to know, the Lord;</hi> for in that day we shall see him be perfected, and yet be eternally increasing. Or, taking it as we read it, <hi type="italic">If we follow on to know,</hi> we have here, [1.] A precious blessing promised: <hi type="italic">Then shall we know,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">know the Lord,</hi> then when <hi type="italic">we return to God;</hi> those that come to God shall be brought into an acquaintance with him. When we are designed to <hi type="italic">live in his sight,</hi> then he gives us to know him; for this is <hi type="italic">life eternal to know God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.3">John xvii. 3</reference>. [2.] The way and means of obtaining this blessing. We must <hi type="italic">follow on to know</hi> him. We must value and esteem the knowledge of God as the best knowledge, we must <hi type="italic">cry after it,</hi> and <hi type="italic">dig for it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.3-Prov.2.4">Prov. ii. 3, 4</reference>), must <hi type="italic">seek and intermeddle with all wisdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.1">Prov. xviii. 1</reference>), and must proceed in our enquiries after this knowledge and our endeavours to improve in it. And, if we do the prescribed duty, we have reason to expect the promised mercy, that we shall know more and more of God, and be at last perfect in this knowledge. <div eID="gen19783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19784" type="x-p"/> (3.) That then they shall abound in divine consolations: <hi type="italic">His going forth is prepared as the morning,</hi> that is, the returns of his favour, which he had withdrawn from us when he went and <hi type="italic">returned to his place.</hi> His out-goings again are prepared and secured to us as firmly as the return of the morning after a dark night, and we expect it, as those do that <hi type="italic">wait for the morning</hi> after a long night, and are sure that it will come at the time appointed and will not fail; and the light of his countenance will be both welcome to us and growing upon us, unto the perfect day, as the light of the morning is. <hi type="italic">He shall come to us,</hi> and be welcome to us, <hi type="italic">as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth,</hi> which refreshes it and makes it fruitful. Now this looks further than their deliverance out of captivity, and, no doubt, was to have its full accomplishment in Christ, and the grace of the gospel. The Old-Testament saints <hi type="italic">followed on to know him,</hi> earnestly looked for redemption in Jerusalem; and at length the out-goings of divine grace in him, in his going forth to visit this world, were [1.] As the morning to this earth when it is dark for he went forth as the <hi type="italic">sun of righteousness,</hi> and in him <hi type="italic">the day-spring from on high visited us. His going forth was prepared as the morning,</hi> for he came in the fulness of time; John Baptist was his fore-runner, nay, he was himself the <hi type="italic">bright and morning star.</hi> [2.] As the rain to this earth when it is <hi type="italic">dry. He shall come down as the rain upon the mown grass,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Ps. lxxii. 6</reference>. In him showers of blessings descend upon this world, which <hi type="italic">give seed to the sower and bread to the eater,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.10">Isa. lv. 10</reference>. And the favour of God in Christ is what is said of the king's favour, <hi type="italic">like the cloud of the latter rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.15">Prov. xvi. 15</reference>. The grace of God in Christ is both the <hi type="italic">latter and the former rain,</hi> for by it the good work of our fruit-bearing is both begun and carried on.
entries.128bc4816241df608f29aa184fa7b66418738d5a: <div eID="gen19784" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises and Expostulations; The Crimes of the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen19785" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? O Judah, what shall I do unto thee? for your goodness <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away. <hi type="super">5</hi> Therefore have I hewed <hi type="italic">them</hi> by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth: and thy judgments <hi type="italic">are as</hi> the light <hi type="italic">that</hi> goeth forth. <hi type="super">6</hi> For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. <hi type="super">7</hi> But they like men have transgressed the covenant: there have they dealt treacherously against me. <hi type="super">8</hi> Gilead <hi type="italic">is</hi> a city of them that work iniquity, <hi type="italic">and is</hi> polluted with blood. <hi type="super">9</hi> And as troops of robbers wait for a man, <hi type="italic">so</hi> the company of priests murder in the way by consent: for they commit lewdness. <hi type="super">10</hi> I have seen a horrible thing in the house of Israel: there <hi type="italic">is</hi> the whoredom of Ephraim, Israel is defiled. <hi type="super">11</hi> Also, O Judah, he hath set a harvest for thee, when I returned the captivity of my people. <div eID="gen19785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19786" type="x-p"/> Two things, two evil things, both Judah and Ephraim are here charged with, and justly accused of:— <div eID="gen19786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19787" type="x-p"/> I. That they were not firm to their own convictions, but were unsteady, <hi type="italic">unstable as water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4-Hos.6.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">O Ephraim! what shall I do unto thee? O Judah! what shall I do unto thee?</hi> This is a strange expression. Can Infinite Wisdom be at a loss what to do? Can it be nonplussed, or put upon taking new measures? By no means; but God speaks after the manner of men, to show how absurd and unreasonable they were, and how just his proceedings against them were. Let them not complain of him as harsh and severe in tearing them, and smiting them, as he has done; for what else should he do? What other course could he take with them? God had tried various methods with them (<hi type="italic">What could have been done more to his vineyard than he had done?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Isa. v. 4</reference>), and very loth he was to let things go to extremity; he reasons with himself (as <reference osisRef="Hos.11.9">ch. xi. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?</hi> God would have done them good, but they were not qualified for it: "<hi type="italic">What shall I do unto thee?</hi> What else can I do but cast thee off, when I cannot in honour save thee?" Note, God never destroys sinners till he sees there is no other way with them. See here, 1. What their conduct was towards God: <hi type="italic">Their goodness,</hi> or <hi type="italic">kindness,</hi> was <hi type="italic">as the morning cloud.</hi> Some understand it of their kindness to themselves and their own souls, in their repentance; it is indeed mercy to ourselves to repent of our sins, but they soon retracted that kindness to themselves, undid it again, and wronged their own souls as much as ever. But it is rather to be taken for their piety and religion; what good appeared in them sometimes, it soon vanished and disappeared again, <hi type="italic">as the morning cloud and the early dew.</hi> Such was the goodness of Israel in Jehu's time, and of Judah in Hezekiah's and Josiah's time; it was soon gone. In time of drought the <hi type="italic">morning-cloud</hi> promises rain, and the <hi type="italic">early dew</hi> is some present refreshment to the earth; but the cloud is dispersed (and hypocrites are compared to <hi type="italic">clouds without water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.12">Jude 12</reference>) and the dew does not soak into the ground, but is drawn back again into the air, and the earth is parched still. What shall he do with them? Shall he accept their goodness? No, for it <hi type="italic">passes away;</hi> and <hi type="italic">factum non dicitur quod non perseverat—that which does not continue can scarcely be said to be done.</hi> Note, That goodness will never be either pleasing to God or profitable to ourselves which is as the morning cloud and the early dew. When men promise fair and do not perform, when they begin well in religion and do not hold on, when they leave their first love and their first works, or, though they do not quite cast off religion, are yet unsteady, uneven, and inconstant in it, then is their <hi type="italic">goodness as the morning cloud and the early dew.</hi> 2. What course God had taken with them (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because they were so rough and ill-shapen, <hi type="italic">I have hewn them by the prophets,</hi> as timber or stone is hewn for use; <hi type="italic">I have slain them by the words of my mouth.</hi>" What the prophets did was done by the word of God in their mouths, which never returned void. By it they thought themselves slain, were ready to say that the prophets killed them, or cut them to the heart when they dealt faithfully with them. (1.) The prophets hewed them by convictions of sin, endeavouring to cut off their transgressions from them. They were uneven in religion (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">v. 4</reference>), therefore God hewed them. The hearts of sinners are not only as stone, but as rough stone, which requires a great deal of pains to bring it into shape, or as knotty timber, that is not squared without a great deal of difficulty; ministers' work is to hew them, and God by the minister hews them, <hi type="italic">for with the froward will he show himself froward.</hi> And there are those whom ministers must rebuke sharply; every word should cut, and though the chips fly in the face of the workman, though the reproved fly in the face of the reprover and reckon him an enemy because he tells the truth, yet he goes on with his work. (2.) They slew them by the denunciations of wrath, foretelling that they should be slain, as Ezekiel is said to destroy the city when he prophesied of the destruction of it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.3">Ezek. xliii. 3</reference>. And God accomplished that which was foretold: "<hi type="italic">I have slain them</hi> by my judgments, according to the words of my mouth." Note, The word of God will be the death either of the sin or of the sinner, a savour either of life unto life or of death unto death. Some read it, "<hi type="italic">I have hewn the prophets, and slain them by the words of my mouth,</hi> that is, I have employed them in laborious service for the people's good, which has wasted their strength; they have spent themselves, and hews away all their spirits, in their work, and in hazardous service, which has cost many of them their lives." Note, Ministers are the tools which God makes use of in working upon people; and, though with many they labour in vain, yet God will reckon for the wearing out of his tools. (3.) God was hereby justified in the severest proceedings against them afterwards. His prophets had taken a great deal of pains with them, had admonished them of their sin and warned them of their danger, but the means used had not the desired effect; some good impressions perhaps were made for the present, but they wore off, and passed away as the morning cloud, and now they cannot charge God with severity if he bring upon them the miseries threatened. The prophet turns to him and acknowledges, <hi type="italic">Thy judgments are as the light that goes forth,</hi> evidently just and righteous. Note, Though sinners be not reclaimed by the pains that ministers take with them, yet thereby God will be <hi type="italic">justified when he speaks and clear when he judges.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Matt.11.17-Matt.11.19">Matt. xi. 17-19</reference>. <div eID="gen19787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19788" type="x-p"/> II. That they were not faithful to God's covenant with them, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6-Hos.6.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen19788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19789" type="x-p"/> 1. What the covenant was that God made with them, and upon what terms they should obtain his favour and be accepted of him (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I desired mercy and not sacrifice</hi> (that is, rather than sacrifice), and insisted upon <hi type="italic">the knowledge of God more than</hi> upon <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings. Mercy</hi> here is the same word which in <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">v. 4</reference> is rendered <hi type="italic">goodness—chesed—piety, sanctity;</hi> it is put for all practical religion; it is the same with <hi type="italic">charity</hi> in the New Testament, the reigning love of God and our neighbour, and this accompanied with and flowing from the <hi type="italic">knowledge of God,</hi> as he has revealed himself in his word, a firm belief that he is, and is the <hi type="italic">rewarder of those that diligently seek him,</hi> a good affection to divine things guided by a good judgment, which cannot but produce a very good conversation; this is that which God by his covenant requires, and <hi type="italic">not sacrifice and offering.</hi> This is fully explained, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.22-Jer.7.23">Jer. vii. 22, 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">I spoke not to your fathers concerning burnt-offerings</hi> (that was the smallest of the matters I spoke to them of, and on which the least stress was laid), but <hi type="italic">this I said, Obey my voice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8">Mic. vi. 6-8</reference>. To love God and our neighbour is <hi type="italic">better than all burnt offering and sacrifice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.12.33">Mark xii. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.16-Ps.51.17">Ps. li. 16, 17</reference>. Not but that sacrifice and offering were required, and to be paid, and had their use, and, when they were accompanied with mercy and the knowledge of God, were acceptable to him, but, without them, God regarded them not, he despised them, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10-Isa.1.11">Isa. i. 10, 11</reference>. Perhaps this is mentioned here to show a difference between the God whom they deserted and the gods whom they went over to. The true God aimed at nothing but that they should be good men, and live good lives for their own good, and the ceremony of honouring him with sacrifices was one of the smallest matters of his law; whereas the false gods required that only; let their priests and altars be regaled with sacrifices and offerings, and the people might live as they listed. What fools were those then that left a God who aimed at giving his worshippers a new nature, for gods who aimed at nothing but making themselves a new name! It is mentioned likewise to show that God's controversy with them was not for the omission of sacrifices (<hi type="italic">I will not reprove thee for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Ps. l. 8</reference>), but because there was no <hi type="italic">justice, nor mercy,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">knowledge of God,</hi> among them (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.1">ch. iv. 1</reference>), and to teach us all that the <hi type="italic">power of godliness</hi> is the main thing God looks at and requires, and without it the <hi type="italic">form of godliness</hi> is of no avail. Serious piety in the heart and life is the <hi type="italic">one thing needful,</hi> and, separate from that, the performances of devotion, though ever so plausible, ever so costly, are of no account. Our Saviour quotes this to show that moral duties are to be preferred before rituals whenever they come in competition, and to justify himself in <hi type="italic">eating with publicans and sinners,</hi> because it was in mercy to the souls of men, and in healing on the sabbath day, because it was in mercy to the bodies of men, to which the ceremony of singularity in eating and the sabbath-rest must give way, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Matt. ix. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.7">xii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen19789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19790" type="x-p"/> 2. How little they had regarded this covenant, though it was so well ordered in all things, though they, and not God, would be the gainers by it. See here what came of it. <div eID="gen19790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19791" type="x-p"/> (1.) In general, they broke with God, and proved unfaithful; there were <hi type="italic">good things committed</hi> to them to keep, the jewels of mercy and piety, and the knowledge of God, in the cabinet of sacrifice and burnt-offering, but they betrayed their trust, kept the cabinet, but pawned the jewels for the gratification of a base lust, and this is that for which God has justly a quarrel with them (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">They, like men, have transgressed the covenant,</hi> that covenant which God made with them; they have broken the conditions of it, and so forfeited the benefit of it. By casting off mercy and the knowledge of God, and other instances of disobedience, [1.] They had contracted the guilt of perjury and covenant-breaking; they were like men that transgress a covenant by which they had solemnly bound themselves, which is a thing that all the world cries out shame on; men that have done so deserve not again to be valued, or trusted, or dealt with. "<hi type="italic">There,</hi> in that thing, <hi type="italic">they have dealt treacherously against me;</hi> they have been perfidious, base, and false children, in whom is no faith, though I depended upon their being <hi type="italic">children that would not lie.</hi>" [2.] In this they had but acted like themselves, <hi type="italic">like men,</hi> who are generally false and fickle, and in whose nature (their corrupt nature) it is to deal treacherously; <hi type="italic">all men are liars,</hi> and they are like the rest of that degenerate race, <hi type="italic">all gone aside,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.14.2-Ps.14.3">Ps. xiv. 2, 3</reference>. They have <hi type="italic">transgressed the covenant</hi> like <hi type="italic">men</hi> (like the Gentiles that transgressed the covenant of nature), like <hi type="italic">mean men</hi> (the word here used is sometimes put for <hi type="italic">men of low degree</hi>); they have dealt deceitfully, like base men that have no sense of honour. [3.] Herein they trod in the steps of our first parents: <hi type="italic">They, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant</hi> (so it might very well be read); as he transgressed the covenant of innocency, so they transgressed the covenant of grace, so treacherously, so foolishly; <hi type="italic">there</hi> in paradise he violated his engagements to God, and there in Canaan, another paradise, they violated their engagements. And by their treacherous dealing they, like Adam, have ruined themselves and theirs. Note, Sin is so much the worse the more there is in it of the <hi type="italic">similitude of Adam's transgression,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.14">Rom. v. 14</reference>. [4.] Low thoughts of God and of his authority and favour were at the bottom of all this; for so some read it: <hi type="italic">They have transgressed the covenant, as of a man,</hi> as if it had been but the covenant of a man, that stood upon even ground with them, as if the commands of the covenant were but like those of a man like themselves, and the kindness conveyed by it no more valuable than that of a man. There is something sacred and binding in <hi type="italic">a man's covenant</hi> (as the apostle shows, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.15">Gal. iii. 15</reference>), but much more in the covenant of God, which yet they made small account of; and <hi type="italic">there</hi> in that covenant they <hi type="italic">dealt treacherously,</hi> promised fair, but performed nothing. Dealing treacherously with God is here called dealing treacherously against him, for it is both an affront and an opposition. Deserters are traitors, and will be so treated; the revolting heart is a rebellious heart. <div eID="gen19791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19792" type="x-p"/> (2.) Some particular instances of their treachery are here given: <hi type="italic">There they dealt treacherously,</hi> that is, in the places hereafter named [1.] Look on the other side Jordan, to the country which lay most exposed to the insults of the neighbouring nations, and where therefore the people were concerned to keep themselves under the divine protection, and yet there you will find the most daring provocations of the divine Majesty, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.8">v. 8</reference>. Gilead, which lay in the lot of Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, was <hi type="italic">a city of the workers of iniquity.</hi> Wickedness was the trade that was driven there; the country was called <hi type="italic">Gilead,</hi> but it was all called a <hi type="italic">city,</hi> because they were all as it were incorporated in one society of rebels against God. Or (as most think) Ramoth Gilead is the city here meant, one of the three cities of refuge on the other side Jordan, and a Levites' city; the inhabitants of it, though of the sacred tribe, were <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity,</hi> contrived it, and practised it. Note, It is bad indeed when a Levites' city is <hi type="italic">a city of those that work iniquity,</hi> when those that are to preach good doctrine live bad lives. Particularly it is <hi type="italic">polluted with blood,</hi> as if that were a sin which the wicked Levites were in a special manner guilty of. In popish countries the clergy are observed to be the most bloody persecutors. Or, as it was a <hi type="italic">city of refuge,</hi> by abusing the power it had to judge of murders it became <hi type="italic">polluted with blood.</hi> They would, for a bribe, protect those that were guilty of wilful murder, whom they ought to have put to death, and would deliver those to the avenger of blood who were guilty but of chance-medley, if they were poor and had nothing to give them; and both these ways they were <hi type="italic">polluted with blood.</hi> Note, Blood defiles the land where it is shed, and where no inquisition is made or no vengeance taken for it. See how the best institutions, that are ever so well designed to keep the balance even between justice and mercy, are capable of being abused and perverted to the manifest prejudice and violation of both. [2.] Look among those whose business it was to minister in holy things, and they were as bad as the worst and as vile as the vilest (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The company of priests</hi> are so, not here and there one that is the scandal of his order, but the whole order and body of them, the <hi type="italic">priests</hi> go all one way <hi type="italic">by consent, with one shoulder</hi> (as the word is), one and all; and they make one another worse, more daring, and fierce, and impudent, in sin, more crafty and more cruel. A <hi type="italic">company of priests</hi> will say and do that in conspiracy which none of them would dare to say or do singly. The <hi type="italic">companies of priests</hi> were as <hi type="italic">troops of robbers,</hi> as <hi type="italic">banditti,</hi> or gangs of highwaymen, that cut men's throats to get their money. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They were cruel and blood-thirsty. They <hi type="italic">murder</hi> those that they have a pique against, or that stand in their way; nothing less will satisfy them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They were cunning. They <hi type="italic">laid wait</hi> for men, that they might have a fair opportunity to compass their mischievous malicious designs; thus the company of priests laid wait for Christ to take him, saying, <hi type="italic">Not on the feast-day. Thirdly,</hi> They were concurring as one man: <hi type="italic">They murder in the way;</hi> in the highway, where travellers should be safe, there <hi type="italic">they murder by consent,</hi> aiding and abetting one another in it. See how unanimous wicked people are in doing mischief; and should not good people be so then in doing good? <hi type="italic">They murder in the way to Shechem</hi> (so the margin reads it, as a proper name) such as were going to Jerusalem (for that way Shechem lay) to worship. Or <hi type="italic">in the way to Shechem</hi> (some think) means in the same manner that their father Levi, with Simeon his brother, murdered the Shechemites (<reference osisRef="Gen.34.1-Gen.34.31">Gen. xxxiv.</reference>), by fraud and deceit; and some understand it of their destroying the souls of men by drawing them to sin. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> They did it with contrivance: <hi type="italic">They commit lewdness;</hi> the word signifies such wickedness as is committed with deliberation, and of malice prepense, as we say. The more there is of device and design in sin the worse it is. [3.] Look into the body of the people, take a view of the whole house of Israel, and they are all alike (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have seen a horrible thing in the house of Israel,</hi> and, though it be ever so artfully managed, God discovers it, and will discover it to them; and who can deny that which God himself says that he has seen? <hi type="italic">There is the whoredom of Ephraim,</hi> both corporal and spiritual whoredom; there it is too plain to be denied. Note, The sin of sinners, especially sinners of the house of Israel, has enough in it to make them tremble, for it is a horrible thing, it is amazing, and it is threatening, enough to make them blush, for Israel is thereby defiled and rendered odious in the sight of God. [4.] Look into Judah, and you find them sharing with Israel (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Also, O Judah! he has set a harvest for thee;</hi> thou must be reckoned with as well as Ephraim; thou art ripe for destruction too, and the time, even the set time, of thy destruction is hastening on, when thou that hast <hi type="italic">ploughed iniquity,</hi> and <hi type="italic">sown wickedness,</hi> shalt <hi type="italic">reap the same.</hi> The general judgment is compared to <hi type="italic">a harvest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.39">Matt. xiii. 39</reference>), so are particular judgments, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.13">Joel iii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Rev. xiv. 15</reference>. I have appointed a time to call thee to account, even <hi type="italic">when I returned the captivity of my people,</hi> that is, when those captives of Judah which were taken by the men of Israel were restored, in obedience to the command of God sent them by Oded the prophet, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.8-2Chr.28.15">2 Chron. xxviii. 8-15</reference>. When God spared them that time he <hi type="italic">set them a harvest,</hi> that is, he designed to reckon with them another time for all together. Note, Preservations from present judgments, if a good use be not made of them, are but reservations for greater judgments.  <chapter eID="Hos.6"/> <div eID="gen19792" type="x-p"/>

entries.c2d630c39785d780cbdbc62cd5976f86af577ccf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12311"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.6.1-Hos.6.11">Ho 6:1-11</reference>. The Israelites' Exhortation to One Another to Seek the Lord.</title> <div sID="gen22461" type="x-p"/> At <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">Ho 6:4</reference> a new discourse, complaining of them, begins; for <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1-Hos.6.3">Ho 6:1-3</reference> evidently belong to <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Ho 5:15</reference>, and form the happy termination of Israel's punishment: primarily, the return from Babylon; ultimately, the return from their present long dispersion. <reference osisRef="Hos.6.8">Ho 6:8</reference> perhaps refers to the murder of Pekahiah; the discourse cannot be later than Pekah's reign, for it was under it that Gilead was carried into captivity (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>).<div eID="gen22461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22462" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12311"/><hi type="bold">1. let us return--</hi>in order that God who has "returned to His place" may return to us (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Ho 5:15</reference>).<div eID="gen22462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">torn, and ... heal--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.39">De 32:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">Jr 30:17</reference>). They ascribe their punishment not to fortune, or man, but to God, and acknowledge that none (not the Assyrian, as they once vainly thought, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Ho 5:13</reference>) but God can heal their wound. They are at the same time persuaded of the mercy of God, which persuasion is the starting-point of true repentance, and without which men would not seek, but hate and flee from God. Though our wound be severe, it is not past hope of recovery; there is room for grace, and a hope of pardon. He hath smitten us, but not so badly that He cannot heal us (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>). <div eID="gen22463" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffec782f07c966d74685063dcbab5c72855bd900: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12312"/><div sID="gen22464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12312"/>2. Primarily, in type, Israel's national revival, in a short period ("two or three" being used to denote a few days, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Is 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.32">Lu 13:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.33">33</reference>); antitypically the language is so framed as to refer in its full accuracy only to Messiah, the ideal Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.3">Is 49:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.2.15">Mt 2:15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>), raised on the third day (<reference osisRef="John.2.19">Joh 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.4">1Co 15:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>). "He shall prolong His days." Compare the similar use of Israel's political resurrection as the type of the general resurrection of which "Christ is the first-fruits" (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Is 26:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.14">Eze 37:1-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live in his sight--</hi>enjoy His favour and the light of His countenance shining on us, as of old; in contrast to <reference osisRef="Hos.5.6">Ho 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">15</reference>, "Withdrawn Himself from them." <div eID="gen22465" type="x-p"/>
entries.b193ba44d9f7a729c89352a4caa12153ea56ab54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12313"/><div sID="gen22466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12313"/><hi type="bold">3. know, if we follow on to know the Lord--</hi>The result of His recovered favor (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.2">Ho 6:2</reference>) will be onward growth in saving knowledge of God, as the result of perseverance in following after Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">Psa 63:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Is 54:13</reference>). "Then" implies the consequence of the revival in <reference osisRef="Hos.6.2">Ho 6:2</reference>. The "if" is not so much conditional, as expressive of the means which God's grace will sanctify to the full enlightenment of Israel in the knowledge of Him. As want of "knowledge of God" has been the source of all evils (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.1">Ho 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.5.4">5:4</reference>), so the knowledge of Him will bring with it all blessings; yea, it is "life" (<reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>). This knowledge is practice, not mere theory (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jr 22:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.16">16</reference>). Theology is life, not science; realities, not words. This onward progress is illustrated by the light of "morning" increasing more and more "unto the perfect day" (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen22466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prepared--</hi>"is sure," literally, "fixed," ordered in His everlasting purposes of love to His covenant-people. Compare "prepared of God" (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.32">Ge 41:32</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.6">Re 12:6</reference>). Jehovah shall surely come to the relief of His people after their dark night of calamity.<div eID="gen22467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the morning--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the rain ... latter ... former--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.29.23">Job 29:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>). First, "the rain" generally is mentioned; then the two rains (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.14">De 11:14</reference>) which caused the fertility of Palestine, and the absence of which was accounted the greatest calamity: "the latter rain" which falls in the latter half of February, and during March and April, just before the harvest whence it takes its name, from a root meaning "to gather"; and "the former rain," literally, "the darting rain," from the middle of October to the middle of December. As the rain fertilizes the otherwise barren land, so God's favor will restore Israel long nationally lifeless. <div eID="gen22469" type="x-p"/>
entries.467fb7fcfc941c9fcb8a6947e40cb0491d385fe8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12314"/><div sID="gen22470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12314"/><hi type="bold">4. what shall I do unto thee--</hi>to bring thee back to piety. What more could be done that I have not done, both in mercies and chastenings (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Is 5:4</reference>)? At this verse a new discourse begins, resuming the threats (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Ho 5:14</reference>). See opening remarks on this chapter.<div eID="gen22470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goodness--</hi>godliness.<div eID="gen22471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">morning cloud--</hi>soon dispersed by the sun (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.3">Ho 13:3</reference>). There is a tacit contrast here to the promise of God's grace to Israel hereafter, in <reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Ho 6:3</reference>. His going forth is "as the morning," shining more and more unto the perfect day; your goodness is "as a morning cloud," soon vanishing. His coming to His people is "as the (fertilizing) latter and former rains"; your coming to Him "as the early dew goeth away." <div eID="gen22472" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe332d717568a8c019c92f137380de8ea71a3ca1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12315"/><div sID="gen22473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12315"/><hi type="bold">5. I hewed them by the prophets--</hi>that is, I announced by the prophets that they should be hewn asunder, like trees of the forest. God identifies His act with that of His prophets; the word being His instrument for executing His will (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jr 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.3">Eze 43:3</reference>).<div eID="gen22473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by ... words of my mouth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.29">Jr 23:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">He 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen22474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22475" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy judgments--</hi>the judgments which I will inflict on thee, Ephraim and Judah (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">Ho 6:4</reference>). So "thy judgments," that is, those inflicted on thee (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.15">Zep 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen22475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are as the light, &c.--</hi>like the light, palpable to the eyes of all, as coming from God, the punisher of sin. Henderson translates, "lightning" (compare Margin, <reference osisRef="Job.37.3">Job 37:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.37.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen22476" type="x-p"/>
entries.2adc39c05aecbbdc390982f36e76f93af69e395a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12316"/><div sID="gen22477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12316"/><hi type="bold">6. mercy--</hi>put for piety in general, of which mercy or charity is a branch.<div eID="gen22477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not sacrifice--</hi>that is, "rather than sacrifice." So "not" is merely comparative (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.8">Ex 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.13">Joe 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.27">Joh 6:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.14">1Ti 2:14</reference>). As God Himself instituted sacrifices, it cannot mean that He desired them not absolutely, but that even in the Old Testament, He valued moral obedience as the only end for which positive ordinances, such as sacrifices, were instituted--as of more importance than a mere external ritual obedience (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Psa 50:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">51:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Is 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8">Mi 6:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Mt 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.7">12:7</reference>).<div eID="gen22478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge of God--</hi>experimental and practical, not merely theoretical (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Ho 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.16">Jr 22:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.3">1Jo 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>). "Mercy" refers to the second table of the law, our duty to our fellow man; "the knowledge of God" to the first table, our duty to God, including inward spiritual worship. The second table is put first, not as superior in dignity, for it is secondary, but in the order of our understanding. <div eID="gen22479" type="x-p"/>
entries.6df8fff6b93565ec504c0ee0e3b975593054283c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12317"/><div sID="gen22480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12317"/><hi type="bold">7. like men--</hi>the common sort of men (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.7">Psa 82:7</reference>). Not as Margin, "like Adam," <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job 31:33</reference>. For the expression "covenant" is not found elsewhere applied to Adam's relation to God; though the thing seems implied (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.12-Rom.5.19">Ro 5:12-19</reference>). Israel "transgressed the covenant" of God as lightly as men break everyday compacts with their fellow men.<div eID="gen22480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there--</hi>in the northern kingdom, Israel. <div eID="gen22481" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddbfb4bb1333a77e3ef11b3577253500c456a55e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12318"/><div sID="gen22482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12318"/><hi type="bold">8. Gilead ... city--</hi>probably Ramoth-gilead, metropolis of the hilly region beyond Jordan, south of the Jabbok, known as "Gilead" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.13">1Ki 4:13</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.31.21-Gen.31.25">Ge 31:21-25</reference>).<div eID="gen22482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work iniquity--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">Ho 12:11</reference>).<div eID="gen22483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">polluted with blood--</hi>"marked with blood-traces" [Maurer]. Referring to Gilead's complicity in the regicidal conspiracy of Pekah against Pekahiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.25">2Ki 15:25</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Ho 6:1</reference>. Many homicides were there, for there were beyond Jordan more cities of refuge, in proportion to the extent of territory, than on this side of Jordan (<reference osisRef="Num.35.14">Nu 35:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.41-Deut.4.43">De 4:41-43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.20.8">Jos 20:8</reference>). Ramoth-gilead was one. <div eID="gen22484" type="x-p"/>
entries.245bb938d628642956fe6a96c1e802f37550138d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12319"/><div sID="gen22485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12319"/><hi type="bold">9. company--</hi>"association" or guild of priests.<div eID="gen22485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">murder by consent--</hi>literally, "with one shoulder" (compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.9">Zep 3:9</reference>, Margin). The image is from oxen putting their shoulders together to pull the same yoke [Rivetus]. Maurer translates, "in the way towards Shechem." It was a city of refuge between Ebal and Gerizim; on Mount Ephraim (<reference osisRef="Josh.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.21">21:21</reference>), long the civil capital of Ephraim, as Shiloh was the religious capital; now called Naploos; for a time the residence of Jeroboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.25">1Ki 12:25</reference>). The priests there became so corrupted that they waylaid and murdered persons fleeing to the asylum for refuge [Henderson]; the sanctity of the place enhanced the guilt of the priests who abused their priestly privileges, and the right of asylum to perpetrate murders themselves, or to screen those committed by others [Maurer].<div eID="gen22486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commit lewdness--</hi>deliberate crime, presumptuous wickedness, from an Arabic root, "to form a deliberate purpose." <div eID="gen22487" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d43a62577ffe9bf156e784d44787e7342385973: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12320"/><div sID="gen22488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12320"/><hi type="bold">10. horrible thing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.30">Jr 5:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.13">18:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.14">23:14</reference>).<div eID="gen22488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whoredom--</hi>idolatry. <div eID="gen22489" type="x-p"/>
entries.f813a85b1d6e832aaa8cd6309e026c8aa54129d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12321"/><div sID="gen22490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12321"/><hi type="bold">11. an harvest--</hi>namely, of judgments (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">Jr 51:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.13">Joe 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Re 14:15</reference>). Called a "harvest" because it is the fruit of the seed which Judah herself had sown (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Ho 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.12">10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pr 22:8</reference>). Judah, under Ahaz, lost a hundred twenty thousand "slain in one day (by Israel under Pekah), because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers."<div eID="gen22490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when I returned the captivity of my people--</hi>when I, by Oded My prophet, caused two hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters, of Judah to be restored from captivity by Israel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.6-2Chr.28.15">2Ch 28:6-15</reference>). This prophecy was delivered under Pekah [Ludovicus De Dieu]. Maurer explains, When Israel shall have been exiled for its sins, and has been subsequently restored by Me, thou, Judah, also shalt be exiled for thine. But as Judah's punishment was not at the time when God restored Israel, Ludovicus De Dieu's explanation must be taken. Grotius translates, "When I shall have returned to make captive (that is, when I shall have again made captive) My people." The first captivity of Israel under Tiglath-pileser was followed by a second under Shalmaneser. Then came the siege of Jerusalem, and the capture of the fenced cities of Judah, by Sennacherib, the forerunner of other attacks, ending in Judah's captivity. But the Hebrew is elsewhere used of restoration, not renewed punishment (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.3">De 30:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference>). <chapter eID="Hos.6"/>

entries.fa857bad28ebe679087494af2796b9475d56444c: <div eID="gen33683" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33684" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33685" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33685" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33684" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33686" type="x-p"/> The prophet earnestly exhorts to repentance, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1-Hos.6.3">Hos 6:1-3</reference>. God is then introduced as very tenderly and pathetically remonstrating against the backslidings of Ephraim and Judah, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4-Hos.6.11">Hos 6:4-11</reference>. <div eID="gen33686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33687" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33688" type="x-p"/> Come, and let us return unto the Lord - When God had purposed to abandon them, and they found that he had returned to his place - to his temple, where alone he could be successfully sought; they, feeling their weakness, and the fickleness, weariness, and unfaithfulness of their idols and allies, now resolve to "return to the Lord;" and, referring to what he said, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Hos 5:14</reference> : "I will tear and go away;" they say, he "hath torn, but he will heal us;" their allies had torn, but they gave them no healing. While, therefore, they acknowledge the justice of God in their punishment, they depend on his well-known mercy and compassion for restoration to life and health.
entries.e37f3021a16209b5d6111f1b6f5f8fbbe4884748: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33689" type="x-p"/> After two days will he revive - Such is his power that in two or three days he can restore us. He can realize all our hopes, and give us the strongest token for good. <div eID="gen33689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33690" type="x-p"/> In the third day he will raise us up - In so short a time can he give us complete deliverance. These words are supposed to refer to the death and resurrection of our Lord; and it is thought that the apostle refers to them, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.4">1Cor 15:4</reference> : "Christ rose again the third day, according to the Scriptures;" and this is the only place in the Scriptures, i.e., of the Old Testament, where his resurrection on the third day seems to be hinted at. The original, יקמנו yekimenu, has been translated, he will raise him up. Then they who trusted in him could believe that they should be quickened together with him. <div eID="gen33690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33691" type="x-p"/> And we shall live in his sight - His resurrection being a proof of theirs.
entries.c1d421b82d0cd2e961cabee0a3f763d1c615eb03: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33692" type="x-p"/> Then shall we know - We shall have the fullest evidence that we have not believed in vain. <div eID="gen33692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33693" type="x-p"/> If we follow on to know the Lord - If we continue to be as much in earnest as we now are. <div eID="gen33693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33694" type="x-p"/> His going forth - The manifestation of his mercy to our souls is as certain as the rising of the sun at the appointed time. <div eID="gen33694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33695" type="x-p"/> And he shall come unto us as the rain - As surely as the early and the latter rain come. The first, to prepare the earth for the seed; this fell in autumn: the second, to prepare the full ear for the harvest; this fell in spring. Here is strong confidence; but not misplaced, however worthless the persons were. As surely as the sun, who is now set, is running his course to arise on us in the morning, and make a glorious day after a dreary night, so surely shall the Lord come again from his place, and the Sun of righteousness shall arise on our souls with healing in his wings. He is already on his way to save us.
entries.1964031a813918142b8ad6413bac6403e0383935: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33696" type="x-p"/> O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? - This is the answer of the Lord to the above pious resolutions; sincere while they lasted, but frequently forgotten, because the people were fickle. Their goodness (for goodness it was while it endured) was like the morning cloud that fadeth away before the rising sun, or like the early dew which is speedily evaporated by heat. Ephraim and Judah had too much goodness in them to admit of their total rejection, and too much evil to admit of their being placed among the children. Speaking after the manner or men, the justice and mercy of Good seem puzzled how to act toward them. When justice was about to destroy them for their iniquity, it was prevented by their repentance and contrition: when mercy was about to pour upon them as penitents its choicest blessings, it was prevented by their fickleness and relapse! These things induce the just and merciful God to exclaim, "O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? O Judah, what shall I do unto thee?" The only thing that could be done in such a case was that which God did.
entries.f5fbfac84715ecfd4628a2a181a18a7259f2a007: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33697" type="x-p"/> Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets - I have sent my prophets to testify against their fickleness. They have smitten them with the most solemn and awful threatenings; they have, as it were, slain them by the words of my mouth. But to what purpose? <div eID="gen33697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33698" type="x-p"/> Thy judgments are as the light that goeth forth - Instead of ומשפטיך אור יצא umispateycha or yetse, "and thy judgments a light that goeth forth," the versions in general have read ומשפטי כאור umishpati keor, "and my judgment is as the light." The final כ caph in the common reading has by mistake been taken from אור aur, and joined to משפטי mishpati; and thus turned it from the singular to the plural number, with the postfix כ cha. The proper reading is, most probably, "And my judgment is as the light going forth." It shall be both evident and swift; alluding both to the velocity and splendour of light.
entries.3a6746758734397c720b5e6548c8f6cb83c343e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33699" type="x-p"/> I desired mercy, and not sacrifice - I taught them righteousness by my prophets; for I desired mercy. I was more willing to save than to destroy; and would rather see them full of penitent and holy resolutions, than behold them offering the best and most numerous victims upon my altar. See <reference osisRef="Mat.9.13">Mat 9:13</reference>.
entries.2b215eeec37ea04369d24f3cc50ed291bb30c1ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33700" type="x-p"/> But they like men (כאדם keadam, "like Adam") have transgressed the covenant - They have sinned against light and knowledge as he did. This is sense, the other is scarcely so. There was a striking similarity in the two cases. Adam, in Paradise, transgressed the commandment, and I cast him out: Israel, in possession of the promised land, transgressed my covenant, and I cast them out, and sent them into captivity.
entries.c33be40e8f2ea6fd5653722aeb27369f7d094abe: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33701" type="x-p"/> Gilead is a city of them that work iniquity - In this place Jacob and Laban made their covenant, and set up a heap of stones, which was called Galeed, the heap of testimony; and most probably idolatry was set up here. Perhaps the very heap became the object of superstitious adoration.
entries.98408918490e9298ed5a2a58e03264a20e6b92f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33702" type="x-p"/> As troops of robbers - What a sad picture is this of the state of the priesthood! The country of Gilead was infamous for its robberies and murders. The idolatrous priests there formed themselves into companies, and kept possession of the roads and passes; and if they found any person going to Jerusalem to worship the true God, they put him to death. The reason is given: - <div eID="gen33702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33703" type="x-p"/> For they commit lewdness - They are gross idolaters.
entries.09b4df852952a2b6f3d976f022569dab426df0b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33704" type="x-p"/> I have seen a horrible thing - That is, the idolatry that prevailed in Israel to such a degree that the whole land was defiled.
entries.b277cc833b6ff354ce47903ad12ad78a6d64b0a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33705" type="x-p"/> O Judah, he hath set a harvest for thee - Thou also hast transgressed; thy harvest will come; thou shalt be reaped down and sent into captivity. The sickle is already thrust in. That which thou hast sowed shalt thou reap. They who sow unto the flesh shall reap corruption. <div eID="gen33705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33706" type="x-p"/> When I returned the captivity of my people - Bp. Newcome translates, "Among those who lead away the captivity of my people." There is thy harvest; they who have led Israel into captivity shall lead thee also into the same. The Assyrians and Babylonians were the same kind of people; equally idolatrous, equally oppressive, equally cruel. From the common reading some suppose this to be a promise of return from captivity. It is true that Judah was gathered together again and brought back to their own land, but the majority of the Israelites did not return, and are not now to be found.  <chapter eID="Hos.6"/> <div eID="gen33706" type="x-p"/>

entries.41ffcaad2c0a0e8a13e7237b10fa2072cec3f3ac: Hos 6:1-3 <div eID="gen16215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16216" type="x-p"/> To this threat the prophet appends in the concluding strophe, both the command to return to the Lord, and the promise that the Lord will raise His smitten nation up again, and quicken them anew with His grace. The separation of these three verses from the preceding one, by the division of the chapters, is at variance with the close connection in the actual contents, which is so perfectly obvious in the allusion made in the words of Hos 6:1, “Come, and let us return,” to those of Hos 5:15, “I will go, and return,” and in טרף וירפּאנוּ (Hos 6:1) to the similar words in Hos 5:13 and Hos 5:14. Hos 6:1. <hi type="italic">“Come, and let us return to Jehovah: for He has torn in pieces, and will heal us; He has smitten, and will bind us up.</hi> Hos 6:2. <hi type="italic">He will quicken us after two days; on the third He will raise us up, that we may live before Him.” </hi> The majority of commentators, following the example of the Chald. and Septuagint, in which לאמר, λέγοντες, is interpolated before לכוּ, have taken the first three verses as an appeal to return to the Lord, addressed by the Israelites in exile to one another. But it would be more simple, and more in harmony with the general style of Hosea, which is characterized by rapid transitions, to take the words as a call addressed by the prophet in the name of the exile. The promise in v. 3 especially is far more suitable to a summons of this kind, than to an appeal addressed by the people to one another. As the endurance of punishment impels to seek the Lord (Hos 5:15), so the motive to return to the Lord is founded upon the knowledge of the fact that the Lord can, and will, heal the wounds which He inflicts. The preterite <hi type="italic">târaph</hi>, as compared with the future <hi type="italic">'etrōph</hi> in Hos 5:14, presupposes that the punishment has already begun. The following יך is also a preterite with the <hi type="italic">Vav consec.</hi> omitted. The Assyrian cannot heal (Hos 5:13); but the Lord, who manifested Himself as Israel’s physician in the time of Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.26">Exo 15:26</reference>), and promised His people healing in the future also (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.39">Deu 32:39</reference>), surely can. The allusion in the word ירפּאנוּ to this passage of Deuteronomy, is placed beyond all doubt by Hos 6:2. The words, “He revives after two days,” etc., are merely a special application of the general declaration, “I kill, and make alive” (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.39">Deu 32:39</reference>), to the particular case in hand. What the Lord there promises to all His people, He will also fulfil upon the ten tribes of Israel. By the definition “after two days,” and “on the third day,” the speedy and certain revival of Israel is set before them. Two and three days are very short periods of time; and the linking together of two numbers following one upon the other, expresses the certainty of what is to take place within this space of time, just as in the so-called numerical sayings in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.3">Amo 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.5.19">Job 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.16">Pro 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15">Pro 30:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.18">Pro 30:18</reference>, in which the last and greater number expresses the highest or utmost that is generally met with. הקים, to raise the dead (<reference osisRef="Job.14.12">Job 14:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.11">Psa 88:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Isa 26:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa 26:19</reference>). “That we may live before Him:” i.e., under His sheltering protection and grace (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.17.18">Gen 17:18</reference>). The earlier Jewish and Christian expositors have taken the numbers, “after two days, and on the third day,” chronologically. The Rabbins consequently suppose the prophecy to refer either to the three captivities, the Egyptian, the Babylonian, and the Roman, which has not ended yet; or to the three periods of the temple of Solomon, of that of Zerubbabel, and of the one to be erected by the Messiah. Many of the fathers, on the other hand, and many of the early Lutheran commentators, have found in them a prediction of the death of Christ and His resurrection on the third day. Compare, for example, <hi type="italic">Calovii Bibl. illustr. ad h. l.</hi>, where this allusion is defended by a long series of undeniably weak arguments, and where a fierce attack is made, not only upon Calvin, who understood these words as “referring to the liberation of Israel from captivity, and the restoration of the church after two days, i.e., in a very short time;” but also upon Grotius, who found, in addition to the immediate historical allusion to the Israelites, whom God would soon liberate from their death-like misery after their conversion, a foretype, in consequence of a special divine indication, of the time “within which Christ would recover His life, and the church its hope.” But any direct allusion in the hope here uttered to the death and resurrection of Christ, is proved to be untenable by the simple words and their context. The words primarily hold out nothing more than the quickening of Israel out of its death-like state of rejection from the face of God, and that in a very short period after its conversion to the Lord. This restoration to life cannot indeed be understood as referring to the return of the exiles to their earthly fatherland; or, at all events, it cannot be restricted to this. It does not occur till after the conversion of Israel to the Lord its God, on the ground of faith in the redemption effected through the atoning death of Christ, and His resurrection from the grave; so that the words of the prophet may be applied to this great fact in the history of salvation, but without its being either directly or indirectly predicted. Even the resurrection of the dead is not predicted, but simply the spiritual and moral restoration of Israel to life, which no doubt has for its necessary complement the reawakening of the physically dead. And, in this sense, our passage may be reckoned among the prophetic utterances which contain the germ of the hope of a life after death, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19-Isa.26.21">Isa 26:19-21</reference>, and in the vision of Ezekiel in <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1">Eze 37:1</reference>-14. <div eID="gen16216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16217" type="x-p"/> That it did not refer to this in its primary sense, and so far as its historical fulfilment was concerned, is evident from the following verse. Hos 6:3. <hi type="italic">“Let us therefore know, hunt after the knowledge of Jehovah. His rising is fixed like the morning dawn, that He may come to us like the rain, and moisten the earth like the latter rain.” </hi>ונדעה נר corresponds to לכוּ ונשׁוּבה in Hos 6:1. The object to נדעה is also את־יהוה, and נדעה is merely strengthened by the addition of נרדּפה לדּעת. The knowledge of Jehovah, which they would hunt after, i.e., strive zealously to obtain, is a practical knowledge, consisting in the fulfilment of the divine commandments, and in growth in the love of God with all the heart. This knowledge produces fruit. The Lord will rise upon Israel like the morning dawn, and come down upon it like fertilizing rain. מוצאו, His (i.e., Jehovah’s) rising, is to be explained from the figure of the dawn (for יצא applied to the rising of the sun, see <reference osisRef="Gen.19.23">Gen 19:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.19.7">Psa 19:7</reference>). The dawn is mentioned instead of the sun, as the herald of the dawning day of salvation (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.58.8">Isa 58:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.60.2">Isa 60:2</reference>). This salvation which dawns when the Lord appears, is represented in the last clause as a shower of rain that fertilizes the land. יורה is hardly a <hi type="italic">kal</hi> participle, but rather the imperfect <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> in the sense of sprinkling. In <reference osisRef="Deut.11.14">Deu 11:14</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.12">Deu 28:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.26.4-Lev.26.5">Lev 26:4-5</reference>), the rain, or the early and latter rain, is mentioned among the blessings which the Lord will bestow upon His people, when they serve Him with all the heart and soul. This promise the Lord will so fulfil in the case of His newly quickened nation, that He Himself will refresh it like a fertilizing rain. This will take place through the Messiah, as <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Psa 72:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> clearly show.
entries.9cf32bb1bc38d0679d2684c27701a5427217e4ed: Hos 6:4 <div eID="gen16217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16218" type="x-p"/> The prophet’s address commences afresh, as in Hos 2:4, without any introduction, with the denunciation of the incurability of the Israelites. Hos 6:4-11 form the first strophe. Hos 6:4. <hi type="italic">“What shall I do to thee, Ephraim? what shall I do to thee, Judah? for your love is like the morning cloud, and like the dew which quickly passes away.” </hi> That this verse is not to be taken in connection with the preceding one, as it has been by Luther (“how shall I do such good to thee?”) and by many of the earlier expositors, is evident from the substance of the verse itself. For <hi type="italic">‛âsâh</hi>, in the sense of doing good, is neither possible in itself, nor reconcilable with the explanatory clause which follows. The <hi type="italic">chesed</hi>, which is like the morning cloud, cannot be the grace of God; for a morning cloud that quickly vanishes away, is, according to Hos 13:3, a figurative representation of that which is evanescent and perishable. The verse does not contain an answer from Jehovah, “who neither receives nor repels the penitent, because though they love God it is only with fickleness,” as Hitzig supposes; but rather the thought, that God has already tried all kinds of punishment to bring the people back to fidelity to Himself, but all in vain (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.1.5-Isa.1.6">Isa 1:5-6</reference>), because the piety of Israel is as evanescent and transient as a morning cloud, which is dispersed by the rising sun. Judging from the chesed in Hos 6:6, chasdekhem is to be understood as referring to good-will towards other men flowing out of love to God (see at Hos 4:1).
entries.965928da5bde2798c060180578f0aaf5a9faec1e: Hos 6:5 <hi type="italic">“Therefore have I hewn by the prophets, slain them by the words of my mouth: and my judgment goeth forth as light.” ‛Al</hi>-<hi type="italic">kēn</hi>, therefore, because your love vanishes again and again, God must perpetually punish. חצב ב does not mean to strike in among the prophets (Hitzig, after the lxx, Syr., and others); but ב is instrumental, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.15">Isa 10:15</reference>, and <hi type="italic">châtsabh</hi> signifies to hew, not merely to hew off, but to hew out or carve. The <hi type="italic">nebhı̄'ı̄m</hi> cannot be false prophets, on account of the parallel “by the words of my mouth,” but must be the true prophets. Through them God had hewed or carved the nation, or, as Jerome and Luther render it, <hi type="italic">dolavi</hi>, i.e., worked it like a piece of hard wood, in other words, had tried to improve it, and shape it into a holy nation, answering to its true calling. “Slain by the words of my mouth,” which the prophets had spoken; i.e., not merely caused death and destruction to be proclaimed to them, but suspended judgment and death over them - as, for example, by Elijah - since there dwells in the word of God the power to kill and to make alive (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa 49:2</reference>). The last clause, according to the Masoretic pointing and division of the words, does not yield any appropriate meaning. משׁפּטיך could only be the judgments inflicted upon the nation; but neither the singular suffix ך for כם (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.4">Isa 10:4</reference>), nor אור יצא, with the singular verb under the כ <hi type="italic">simil</hi>. omitted before אור, suits this explanation. For אור יצא cannot mean “to go forth to the light;” nor can אור stand for לאור. We must therefore regard the reading expressed by the ancient versions,<note placement="foot">The Vulgate in some of the ancient mss has also judicium meum, instead of the judicia tua of the Sixtina. See Kennicott, Diss. gener. ed. Bruns. p. 55ff.</note> viz., משׁפּטי כאור ציצא, “my judgment goeth forth like light,” as the original one. My penal judgment went forth like the light (the sun); i.e., the judgment inflicted upon the sinners was so obvious, so conspicuous (clear as the sun), that every one ought to have observed it and laid it to heart (cf. Zep 3:5). The Masoretic division of the words probably arose simply from an unsuitable reminiscence of Psa 37:6.
entries.aa02b7d61e81c165b4fee7659cac45f790e60939: Hos 6:6-7 <div eID="gen16218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16219" type="x-p"/> The reason why God was obliged to punish in this manner is given in the following verses. Hos 6:6. <hi type="italic">“For I take pleasure in love, and not in sacrifices; and in the knowledge of God more than in burnt-offerings.</hi> Hos 6:7. <hi type="italic">But they have transgressed the covenant like Adam: there have they acted treacherously towards me.” Chesed</hi> is love to one’s neighbour, manifesting itself in righteousness, love which has its roots in the knowledge of God, and therefore is connected with “the knowledge of God” here as in Hos 4:1.
